newsitem.title: GERMANY: OPINION - US rates slow EU rate convergence.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - US rates slow EU rate convergence.

text.p: By Egbert Sauer, Bond Analyst at DG Bank in Frankfurt
FRANKFURT, Germany (April 23) - The convergence of interest rates in member states of the future European monetary union has been one of the most striking developments of the past few years.
The decrease in the difference in yields in potential EMU member countries, compared to German capital market interest rates, began as early as December 1995 and has continued into the current year.
The decrease was supported by a continuing convergence of the fundamental economic data in all the Western European countries.
The rate of inflation has gone down all over Europe and, in Spain, inflation reached its lowest level for three decades.
The incentive to be among the founding members of European monetary union was strong enough to move the governments to noticeable saving efforts.
Many countries came significantly closer to the Maastricht criteria in this way.
The convergence of yield levels was also driven forward by political determination to keep up the consolidation efforts at least until the start of monetary union.

In some cases, the difference from the yield in the German bond market was even reduced by over 3 percentage points within one year, although it is far from certain if these countries in particular will be able to participate in EMU from 1999.
The rapid interest rate convergence was encouraged by the favourable environment provided by the past two years.
Two events in the nineties show that that can suddenly change.
Mexico's deficit payment crisis at the beginning of 1995 quickly affected all the international bond markets.
Investors reacted by escaping to safe asset havens and thus the European interest rates outside Germany and Switzerland rose.

The second example of an unfavourable economic environment is that in Italy, the yield gap for 10-year bonds increased by 150 basis points in one month. This continued a development that had already begun at the end of January 1994.

Most investors remember the losses in the bond markets in German and the U.S. only too well and have learned that the bond markets outside safe-haven areas are affected the most by interest rate rises.
Now, when monetary union is no longer far off, such a market reaction would be rational, as many countries have mainly short-term debts.
An interest rate increase on short-term debts has an immediate negative effect on the public interest burden, which in turn makes it more difficult to check public debt.
The most recent increase in the target for the Federal Funds Rate to 5.5 percent has caused a swing in opinion.
Many former interest rate optimists now expect a series of key interest rate rises by the Fed, which will lead to a lasting phase with increasing yields in the capital market.

Although we only expect one or two further steps by the Fed to 5.75 or six percent and a moderate increase in capital market interest rates this year, we do expect nervousness to cause a further rise in the long-term interest rates in the US in the coming months.
This will make the environment for interest rate convergence in the euro-area increasingly unfavourable, which should at least slow it down.

Experiences of the past year support this: As the yields in the U.S. and in Germany rose sharply at the beginning of 1996, interest rate convergence came to a halt, although the economic data was coming more into line.
The same was repeated at the beginning of 1997.
Otherwise, European interest rates could continue coming into line with each other, even if the long-term U.S. interest rates moderately rose.
DG Bank does not expect clear signals from the euro countries, which could outweigh the impact of external interest rate influences.
Examples of this would be if it was decided to delay monetary union or if individual countries decided to give up in the race to participate in time.
We do expect, however, that the group of participants will remain open into April 1998.
The EU Commission convergence report will make clear for the first time whether there are countries that do not meet even generously interpreted Maastricht criteria.

In this case, we would expect a rapid interest rate increase in those countries, which would soon develop into a new convergence process, as supporting measures will offer the affected countries the possiblity of entry as soon as possible.
